QF.id: IV Fixed Income Instruments and Bond Markets_47

question.text: A bank expects long-term bond yields to fall significantly over the next 6 months. Using the standard price-yield/duration relationship, to maximize price gains on its bond portfolio it should:

answer.text: Reduce portfolio duration by selling long bonds
Increase portfolio duration by buying long-maturity bonds
Switch from bonds to money market instruments

explanation.text: The Logic: Bond prices move inversely to yields, and longer-maturity bonds have higher duration and therefore higher price sensitivity to yield changes. If long-term yields are expected to fall, the bank maximizes price gains by lengthening duration - that is, by buying long-maturity bonds (option B). This is the standard price-yield/duration relationship set out on pp.63, 68 and 161 of the NISM Series IV workbook. The Trap: Option A reduces duration and therefore reduces price gains from a yield fall. Option C exits bonds entirely and forgoes the price gain. Option D ignores the rate view. The audit flagged that p.187 of the same workbook contains an internally inconsistent sentence (saying managers lengthen duration if they expect rates to "increase"), which is contrary to the price-yield examples on pp.63 and 68; that page-187 sentence appears to be a workbook error. Note: The original question was ambiguous because p.187 of the workbook conflicts with the workbook's own price-yield examples on pp.63 and 68. The stem has been tightened to anchor the answer to the price-yield/duration relationship and to long-term yields specifically, so option B is uniquely correct. Source: NISM Series IV, Dec 2025, pp.63, 68, 161.
